papers.title: Liposome-Supplemented Cell-free Synthesis of a Peptide that Forms β-barrel Nanopores.
papers.abstract: Rational design of nanopore-forming proteins and peptides is a promising approach for single-molecule analysis by using custom-designed nanopores tailored to specific target molecules. One challenge in this approach is the expression or synthesis of the designed nanopores, due to their high hydrophobicity. We sought to streamline the synthesis of an artificial and highly aggregative nanopore-forming peptide using liposome-supplemented cell-free protein synthesis. By optimizing the liposomal lipid composition, we recovered yields of the expressed aggregative peptide that were suitable for funct
papers.summary: The authors developed a cell-free protein synthesis system supplemented with liposomes to produce a highly hydrophobic, aggregation-prone artificial peptide that forms β-barrel nanopores. By optimizing the liposomal lipid composition, they achieved yields sufficient for functional characterization of the designed nanopore. This streamlines the production of custom-designed nanopores for single-molecule sensing applications.

papers.title: Persistent Local Laplacian Prediction of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinities.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of protein-ligand binding affinity remains a central challenge in structure-based drug discovery. The effectiveness of machine learning models critically depends on the quality of molecular representations, for which advanced mathematical frameworks provide powerful tools. In this work, we employ a novel mathematical theory, termed the persistent local Laplacian (PLL), to construct molecular descriptors that capture localized geometric and topological features of biomolecular structures. The PLL framework addresses key limitations of traditional topological data analysis me
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: The authors introduce a new mathematical framework called the persistent local Laplacian (PLL) to build molecular descriptors that capture local geometric and topological features of protein-ligand complexes. These descriptors are used to train machine learning models for predicting binding affinity, aiming to improve on traditional topological data analysis methods. The work addresses the need for better molecular representations in structure-based drug discovery.

papers.title: Unique features of EIGHT fold-Proteins with the most complex 83 knotted topology.
papers.abstract: Herein, we present three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein to date, an [Formula: see text] knot with eight crossings, which belongs to a clasp knot family. The fold of this protein is also unique, and we call it the EIGHT fold (Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold). The [Formula: see text] knot is found only in a certain group of bacteria, where it is strictly conserved, despite sequence identities as low as 10%. The [Formula: see text] structure shows a high level of internal symmetry, with structurally analogous halves. It is possible that the EIGHT fo
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.summary: The authors report three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein known to date, featuring an 8-crossing knot (a clasp knot) and a novel fold they term the EIGHT fold. This knot is strictly conserved in a specific bacterial group despite sequence identities as low as 10%, and the structure exhibits high internal symmetry with structurally analogous halves.

papers.title: Ultrasound-enhanced co-fermentation of Yunnan Arabica coffee with rose petals: Mass transfer, microbial succession, and molecular modeling.
papers.abstract: Plant-based co-fermentation can diversify coffee flavor profiles, yet multiphase systems are often limited by interfacial mass-transfer resistance and stochastic microbial succession. Here, we investigated the effects of non-thermal pulsed ultrasound (20 kHz, 0.5 W mL-1, 50 % duty cycle, 30 ± 0.5 °C) on the co-fermentation of Yunnan Arabica coffee with Rosa 'Crimson Glory' petals. Acoustic-assisted processing enhanced the apparent solid-liquid mass-transfer rate constant (kobs = 0.082 min-1) and accelerated acidification kinetics. Rheological and acoustic-attenuation monitoring identified 60 %
papers.summary: This study shows that non-thermal pulsed ultrasound speeds up the co-fermentation of Yunnan Arabica coffee with rose petals by improving solid-liquid mass transfer and accelerating acidification. The authors combine rheology, acoustic-attenuation monitoring, and molecular modeling to track microbial succession and fermentation dynamics in this multiphase system.

papers.title: Oleanolic acid-hesperetin co-assembled nanoparticles alleviate neurological injury after ischemic stroke via the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β axis.
papers.abstract: Ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability, while the current clinically applicable adjunctive neuroprotective strategies face substantial limitations. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin exhibit synergistic antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic activities; however, their poor aqueous solubility and limited bioavailability remain major limitations to their therapeutic development. Oleanolic acid and hesperetin were formulated as co-assembled nanoparticles using an emulsion-solvent evaporation method. A 5:2 mass ratio of oleanolic acid to hesperetin produce
papers.summary: This study formulates oleanolic acid and hesperetin into co-assembled nanoparticles to overcome their poor solubility and bioavailability, and tests whether the formulation protects against neurological injury after ischemic stroke. The authors report that the nanoparticles alleviate neurological damage via modulation of the PI3K/AKT/GSK-3β signaling axis, suggesting a potential neuroprotective adjunct strategy.

papers.title: Molecular insights into GPR55 modulation reveal an atypical activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent efficacy regulation.
papers.abstract: GPR55 is a lipid-activated G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) implicated in metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) species are proposed as endogenous agonists, but progress in understanding GPR55 function has still been limited by suboptimal chemical probes. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GPR55 in both inactive and active states. The inactive-state structure bound to the inverse agonist CID16020046 facilitated the rational design of an improved in vitro tool compound, BI-8310. Surprisingly, mutation of a glycosylation s
papers.summary: The authors solved cryo-EM structures of the lipid receptor GPR55 in both inactive and active states, revealing an atypical activation mechanism. The inactive structure bound to an inverse agonist enabled rational design of an improved tool compound, BI-8310. They also found that glycosylation regulates the receptor's efficacy, providing new insight into how GPR55 signaling can be modulated.

papers.title: Biochemistry of protozoan Metacaspases: Structure, processing, and inhibition.
papers.abstract: Metacaspases are calcium-dependent cysteine proteases (clan CD, family C14) present in fungi, protozoa, and plants but absent from mammals. Although structurally related to metazoan caspases, they differ in substrate specificity (cleaving after arginine or lysine), calcium-dependent activation, and monomeric architecture. In protozoan parasites such as Trypanosoma brucei, T. cruzi, Leishmania spp., Plasmodium spp., and Toxoplasma gondii, metacaspases regulate programmed cell death, cell cycle progression, protein quality control, differentiation, and virulence. Their absence in humans and esse
papers.summary: This review examines metacaspases, calcium-dependent cysteine proteases found in protozoan parasites, fungi, and plants but absent in mammals. It covers their structure, activation by calcium, substrate specificity (cleavage after arginine or lysine), and roles in programmed cell death, cell cycle control, protein quality control, differentiation, and virulence in pathogens like Trypanosoma, Leishmania, Plasmodium, and Toxoplasma. Because humans lack these enzymes, the authors highlight their potential as selective drug targets.

papers.title: Innovative design and development of novel thiazole-paracetamol hybrids as COX inhibitors and immunomodulatory activity: design, synthesis, SAR, in vitro biological evaluation, and molecular docking analysis.
papers.abstract: The hybridization approach was employed to design a single pharmacophore based on the conjugation of paracetamol with thiazole derivatives, yielding thiazole-paracetamol hybrid derivatives 4-11 that utilize a linker from hydrazone (-C[double bond, length as m-dash]N-NH) and azo (-N[double bond, length as m-dash]N-) linkers, serving as the hydrogen bond donor/acceptor binding site. The structure of the designed derivatives was fully characterized and confirmed using analytical data (IR, 1H NMR, and 13C NMR), and elemental analysis. The anti-inflammatory potential of the synthesized hybrids was
papers.summary: This study designed and synthesized a series of thiazole-paracetamol hybrid molecules linked via hydrazone or azo groups, aiming to combine anti-inflammatory (COX inhibition) and immunomodulatory activities in a single pharmacophore. The compounds were chemically characterized and evaluated in vitro for biological activity, with structure-activity relationships and molecular docking used to rationalize binding to COX enzymes. The work represents a medicinal chemistry effort to develop dual-action anti-inflammatory agents.

papers.title: RAF isoform selectivity of MEK inhibitors and rational design of a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor.
papers.abstract: Aberrant activation of the RAS/RAF/mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway is a frequent cause of cancer. Allosteric MEK inhibitors block this pathway by binding RAF-MEK complexes to prevent activation of MEK by RAF. However, how MEK inhibitor potency varies across the three RAF isoforms remains poorly understood. We profiled seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and observed a notable hierarchy of sensitivity: All most potently inhibited CRAF-driven MEK activation while relatively sparing ARAF-driven activation. We identified point mutations in AR
papers.summary: The study profiles seven allosteric MEK inhibitors and finds a consistent potency hierarchy across RAF isoforms, with CRAF-driven MEK activation being most strongly inhibited and ARAF-driven activation relatively spared. By mapping the structural basis of this selectivity, the authors rationally design a covalent ARAF-MEK inhibitor that overcomes the ARAF-sparing limitation, offering a strategy to target ARAF-driven tumors.

papers.title: A recyclable [DABCO][Imi]2 deep eutectic solvent for multicomponent synthesis of 1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitriles: in vitro antiproliferative and in silico molecular evaluation.
papers.abstract: This study reports the synthesis of a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES), [DABCO][Imi]2, for the multicomponent synthesis of 2-oxo-4,6-disubstituted-1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitrile derivatives. A novel DES was successfully synthesized and structurally characterized using 1H NMR, 13C NMR, FT-IR spectroscopy, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). A series of 30 derivatives was synthesized in moderate isolated yields (up to 40%). The synthesized compounds were evaluated for their inhibitory activity against human melanoma A375 cancer cells. Among the synthesized compounds, (5cg) and (5ch) exhib
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a new deep eutectic solvent, [DABCO][Imi]2, and used it as a recyclable reaction medium for multicomponent synthesis of 30 1,2-dihydropyridine-3-carbonitrile derivatives, achieving moderate yields (up to 40%). Two compounds showed antiproliferative activity against human melanoma A375 cells, and in silico molecular evaluation was performed. The work is a narrow medicinal chemistry study combining green solvent design with preliminary anticancer screening.

papers.title: How Many Crystal Structures Do You Need to Trust Your Docking Results?
papers.abstract: Structure-based drug discovery relies on the prediction of protein-bound poses of new molecule designs, the accuracy of which can impact downstream prioritization. While it is expected that crystal structures of similar molecules would provide the best template for predicting the poses of new designs, the time and cost required motivates identifying a point of diminishing returns for collecting new structures. Using 403 crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 main protease from the open science COVID Moonshot project, we explore the tradeoff between the cost and utility of obtaining crystal structure
papers.summary: Using 403 crystal structures of SARS-CoV-2 main protease from the COVID Moonshot project, the authors quantify how many experimental structures are needed before additional crystal structures stop improving docking pose prediction accuracy. They identify a point of diminishing returns, offering practical guidance on when collecting more structures is no longer worth the cost for structure-based drug design.

papers.title: Chemical Constituents of Halophyte Suaeda glauca and Their Anti-Adipogenic and Anti-Inflammatory Activities.
papers.abstract: Halophytes are recognized as rich sources of secondary metabolites with a wide range of biological activities. To explore the phytochemical constituents and biological activities of Korean halophytes, we investigated Suaeda glauca, a salt-tolerant species belonging to the family Amaranthaceae. In traditional Chinese medicine, S. glauca has been used to reduce fever and alleviate food retention, and it has also been consumed as a food source. In the present study, we conducted a phytochemical investigation of the aerial parts of S. glauca. Column chromatographic separation of the CH2Cl2-soluble
papers.summary: The authors performed a phytochemical investigation of the halophyte Suaeda glauca, isolating secondary metabolites from its aerial parts via column chromatography and testing them for anti-adipogenic and anti-inflammatory activities. The study identifies chemical constituents of this salt-tolerant plant and reports their bioactivity, supporting its traditional medicinal and dietary uses.

papers.title: Competing Isomerization Channels and Rotor Selectivity in a Third-Generation Molecular Motor: Insights from Nonadiabatic Dynamics.
papers.abstract: Third-generation light-driven molecular motors, characterized by a unique double-rotor architecture, represent a pivotal advancement in nanotechnology. Recently, a novel third-generation molecular motor based on bridged-isoindigo has been proposed. However, the microscopic mechanism behind its ultrafast photoisomerization remains to be explored. In this work, nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations at the semiempirical OM2/MRCI level were employed to investigate the excited-state dynamics of a third-generation molecular motor, starting from the E S Z S configuration. The simulation reveals
papers.summary: This study uses nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the excited-state photoisomerization mechanism of a third-generation light-driven molecular motor based on bridged-isoindigo. The simulations reveal competing isomerization channels and rotor selectivity, providing microscopic insight into the ultrafast dynamics that govern the motor's operation.

papers.title: Antibacterial Activity of Equisetin from Endophytic Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 Associated with Jatropha multifida L. Against MRSA: Experimental and In Silico Insights.
papers.abstract: An antibacterial metabolite was isolated from the endophytic fungus Fusarium incarnatum JMB4 associated with Jatropha multifida L. by bioactivity-guided chromatography and recrystallization. The isolated compound was assigned as equisetin using UV-vis, FTIR, LC-MS/MS, and 1H NMR data. Anti-MRSA activity was evaluated by disk diffusion, with chloramphenicol and amoxicillin as antibiotic comparators. At 1% (w/v; 100 μg/disk), equisetin produced an inhibition zone of 23.94 ± 0.66 mm; the recorded comparator zones were 24.71 ± 0.68 mm for chloramphenicol (30 μg/disk) and 11.76 ± 0.66 mm for amoxic
papers.summary: Researchers isolated equisetin, an antibacterial compound, from an endophytic fungus (Fusarium incarnatum JMB4) living inside the medicinal plant Jatropha multifida. Equisetin showed strong activity against MRSA in disk diffusion assays, producing inhibition zones comparable to chloramphenicol and much larger than amoxicillin. The study combines experimental isolation and testing with in silico (computational) analyses to support the findings.

papers.title: Effects of Coal Rank on the Adsorption Characteristics and Mechanism of Hydrogen Sulfide by Coal Molecules.
papers.abstract: This study systematically investigates the molecular structural characteristics of different rank coals (anthracite, bituminous, lignite) and their adsorption properties and mechanisms toward hydrogen sulfide (H2S). By combining X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and solid-state 13C NMR spectroscopy, it was found that aromatic carbon content increases remarkably from 55.91 to 91.75% with coal rank increasing, whereas aliphatic carbon and oxygen-bearing functional groups decrease accordingly. Macromolecular model representatives corresponding to each coal rank were constructed based on expe
papers.summary: The study characterizes how coal rank (lignite, bituminous, anthracite) affects H2S adsorption, using XPS and solid-state 13C NMR to show that aromatic carbon rises from ~56% to ~92% with rank while aliphatic and oxygen-bearing groups decline. Molecular models built for each rank reveal that higher-rank coals adsorb H2S differently, linking structural composition to adsorption mechanism. This has implications for H2S management in coal mining and coalbed gas.

papers.title: Machine Learning in Amyloidogenic Polypeptide Research: From Sequence Prediction to Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) has established a transformative paradigm for investigating amyloidogenic polypeptides. Characterized by their propensity to form ordered, β-sheet-rich fibrillar aggregates, these polypeptides are centrally implicated in the pathogenesis of numerous neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). This review systematically evaluates the application of ML across critical domains of amyloid investigation: sequence-based amyloidogenicity prediction, structural biology, inhibitor design, and amyloid-related cl
papers.summary: This review surveys how machine learning has been applied across amyloid research, from predicting amyloidogenic sequences to structural characterization and inhibitor/drug design for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. It organizes the field into key application domains and evaluates the methods used in each.

papers.title: Discovery of 2-(2-Benzoyl-5-Phenyl-1H-Imidazol-1-Yl) Derivatives as Inhibitors of Factor XIIa.
papers.abstract: Factor XIIa (FXIIa) has emerged as a promising target for thrombo-inflammatory disorders due to its central role in the intrinsic coagulation cascade and kallikrein-kinin system, coupled with the absence of a bleeding phenotype in FXII deficiency. We report a focused library of 2-(2-benzoyl-5-phenyl-1H-imidazol-1-yl)acetamide derivatives as novel small-molecule FXIIa inhibitors. A series of 23 compounds was synthesized via a concise four-step strategy and evaluated using a chromogenic assay. Several analogues exhibited moderate inhibition, with inhibitor 6 as the most active (IC50 = 120 μM). T
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a small library of 23 imidazole-based compounds and tested them as inhibitors of Factor XIIa, a coagulation protein targeted for treating thrombo-inflammatory disorders without causing bleeding risk. The most potent compound inhibited FXIIa only weakly (IC50 = 120 μM), so this is an early exploratory hit-finding study rather than a therapeutic advance.

papers.title: Three Distinct Binding Modes Govern High-Affinity Ligand Interactions with Amyloid Fibrils.
papers.abstract: Fibrillar protein aggregates are a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases and represent attractive biomarkers and therapeutic targets. However, the rational design of small-molecule ligands and probes targeting these aggregates is limited by a poor understanding of how ligands bind to amyloid fibrils. This work outlines an experimental approach to determine the binding mode of ligands to amyloid fibrils using previously overlooked information contained within standard binding assays. Using a mathematical framework to analyze binding behavior, three distinct high-affinity binding modes
papers.summary: This paper introduces an experimental and mathematical framework to classify how small molecules bind to amyloid fibrils, using overlooked information from standard binding assays. The authors identify three distinct high-affinity binding modes, which could improve the rational design of diagnostic probes and therapeutics targeting neurodegenerative disease aggregates.

papers.title: PDKE-G: A Bio-Inspired Contributory Group Authenticated Key Exchange Grounded in Per-Member AlphaFold2 Protein Geometry.
papers.abstract: Authenticated key exchange underpins secure communication, yet the structural complexity of biological macromolecules has rarely served as cryptographic material. The recently proposed Protein-Derived Key Exchange (PDKE) protocol binds AlphaFold2-predicted protein geometry to ephemeral elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman for two parties. We introduce PDKE-G, a contributory group authenticated key exchange in which each member's signing credential is derived from its protein geometry as a member-specific input: the long-term signing key is extracted with HKDF from the protein's Cα-Cα distance matrix
papers.summary: PDKE-G extends the Protein-Derived Key Exchange protocol from two-party to contributory group authenticated key exchange, where each member's long-term signing credential is derived via HKDF from the Cα–Cα distance matrix of an AlphaFold2-predicted protein structure. The work demonstrates that predicted protein geometry can serve as cryptographic material for multi-party secure communication. It is a proof-of-concept bridging structural bioinformatics and cryptography.

papers.title: Simulating Transport Across the Blood-Brain Barrier Endothelial Membrane: Comparing Unbiased Molecular Dynamics Methods to Enhanced Sampling Protocols.
papers.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective membrane that restricts the delivery of therapeutics into the brain. In this review, we consider a number of computational techniques that can be used to assess BBB transport and central nervous system (CNS) delivery. We outline the details of human brain microvascular endothelial cells (hBMECs) and how passive transport is the main mode of transport. We then outline details of molecular dynamics techniques for predicting in silico drug permeability across an atomistic hBMEC model. Due to the very slow timescales required to sample CNS transp
papers.summary: This review compares computational methods for simulating how drug molecules cross the blood-brain barrier, focusing on molecular dynamics approaches ranging from unbiased simulations to enhanced sampling protocols. It describes the biology of human brain microvascular endothelial cells and argues that passive transport is the dominant route, then evaluates which in silico techniques best predict drug permeability across an atomistic membrane model. The work serves as a practical guide for choosing simulation strategies when studying CNS drug delivery.

papers.title: Mapping Ligand-Induced Conformational Changes during the Enzymatic Cycle of Human Geranylgeranyl Diphosphate Synthase.
papers.abstract: Geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) catalyzes the condensation reaction between two isoprenoid substrates: farnesyl diphosphate (FDP) and isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP), to form geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGDP). Due to the flexible nature of the GGDPS active site and its capacity to bind multiple ligands during the reaction coordinate, understanding the structural changes that enable it to accommodate different ligands and catalyze the reaction is essential. While structures exist of substrate and product-bound GGDPS, a lack of high-resolution apo or Mg2+-only structures prevents com
papers.summary: This study maps the conformational changes in human geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase (GGDPS) as it binds substrates and cofactors during its enzymatic cycle. By obtaining high-resolution structures of the apo and Mg2+-bound states, the authors reveal how the flexible active site rearranges to accommodate farnesyl diphosphate and isopentenyl pyrophosphate. These findings clarify the structural basis for catalysis and may inform drug design targeting GGDPS.

papers.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics
papers.summary: This study presents substrate-bound crystal structures of yeast aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), the enzyme that initiates heme biosynthesis, combined with molecular dynamics simulations. The structures reveal protein dynamics that accompany substrate binding and help explain how ALAS homologs with ~70% sequence similarity diverge functionally. These findings provide a structural basis for understanding ALAS regulation and the effects of disease-causing mutations.

papers.title: Harnessing the ubiquitin-proteasome system: advances and challenges of PROTACs in breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most significant health issues in the world, and resistance to treatment and a lack of targets that can be addressed with drugs limit the effectiveness of the existing treatment options. The development of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) has shifted the concept of occupancy-based inhibition toward event-based targeted protein degradation. Avoiding ubiquitin-proteasome hijacking, PROTACs target disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases, allowing them to be catalytically degraded, thereby eliminating formerly undruggable or resistant targets. Their modular desi
papers.summary: This review discusses proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) as an emerging therapeutic strategy for breast cancer, shifting from occupancy-based inhibition to event-based targeted protein degradation. PROTACs recruit disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases for catalytic degradation, potentially addressing previously undruggable or treatment-resistant targets. The authors highlight advances and remaining challenges in applying this modular technology to breast cancer.

papers.title: From whole-exome sequencing to functional insight: Characterization of rare germline variants in lung cancer.
papers.abstract: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) has greatly expanded the identification of rare germline variants in hereditary cancer predisposition. However, the interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (VUS), particularly in novel candidate genes, remains a major challenge in lung cancer genetics.
papers.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of interpreting rare germline variants of uncertain significance (VUS) identified through whole-exome sequencing in lung cancer predisposition. It characterizes these variants and attempts to move from sequencing data toward functional insight, likely by combining computational and experimental approaches to assess pathogenicity in novel candidate genes.

papers.title: Designing Cooperative Molecular Glues for FKBP12-MAPRE1 with Enhanced-Sampling Molecular Dynamics Simulations.
papers.abstract: Molecular glues (MGs) offer a unique modality for inducing protein-protein interactions (PPIs), yet their rational design is often hindered by the limitations of static structural data. Here, we present a computational pipeline for the design of cooperative MGs for the FKBP12-MAPRE1 system using replica exchange with solute scaling (REST2) for enhanced sampling in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. By sampling the conformational ensembles of binary and ternary complexes, we identified a "stabilized configurational space" that facilitates ternary-complex formation through a combination of con
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.summary: This study presents a computational pipeline for designing molecular glues that induce protein-protein interactions between FKBP12 and MAPRE1, using enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics (REST2) to capture conformational ensembles rather than relying on static structures. By analyzing binary and ternary complex ensembles, the authors identify a 'stabilized configurational space' that promotes ternary-complex formation through cooperative binding effects. The work offers a rational design strategy for molecular glues targeting PPIs.

papers.title: Hydrophobic Hydration at Fluorinated and Hydrocarbon Self-Assembled Monolayers Investigated by In Situ Soft X-Ray Emission Spectroscopy and Molecular Dynamics Simulation.
papers.abstract: We investigated the hydrogen-bonding state and spatial distribution of water at hydrophobic self-assembled monolayer (SAM) interfaces formed by fluoroalkyl and hydrocarbon chains using in situ soft X-ray emission spectroscopy (XES) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations under controlled humidity conditions. Under low water coverage, the hydrocarbon-based SAM exhibited spectral features attributed to isolated water molecules, while the fluorinated SAM showed signatures indicative of tetrahedrally coordinated hydrogen-bond networks. MD simulations revealed that water molecules at the fluorinate
papers.journal: Langmuir : the ACS journal of surfaces and colloids
papers.summary: This study uses soft X-ray emission spectroscopy and molecular dynamics simulations to compare how water molecules arrange at fluorinated versus hydrocarbon self-assembled monolayer surfaces under controlled humidity. The hydrocarbon surface shows isolated water molecules at low coverage, while the fluorinated surface promotes tetrahedrally coordinated hydrogen-bond networks, indicating that fluorination alters interfacial water structure. The findings clarify how surface chemistry controls hydrophobic hydration at the molecular level.

papers.title: Development of REC1: A Reverse Vaccinology-Derived Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Brucellosis.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brucellosis is a widespread intracellular zoonosis that continues to impose substantial public-health and economic burdens in endemic regions. No human brucellosis vaccine has yet been approved, and most existing multi-epitope candidates rely solely on computational predictions, without population-specific human leukocyte antigen (HLA) optimization or in vivo epitope validation. REC1 is therefore an early-stage, proof-of-concept, human-oriented multi-epitope candidate, with epitopes screened against high-frequency HLA alleles in the Chinese population. This study develop
papers.summary: REC1 is a computational multi-epitope vaccine candidate against brucellosis, designed using reverse vaccinology with epitopes selected to match high-frequency HLA alleles in the Chinese population. The work is an early-stage proof-of-concept that relies on computational predictions rather than in vivo validation, and no human brucellosis vaccine has yet been approved.

papers.title: GDEE: A Structure-Based Platform for Gene Discovery and Enzyme Engineering.
papers.abstract: Enzymes are extensively utilized for catalyzing the production of value-added compounds in diverse sectors with significant economic impact. However, challenges such as poor protein expression, low catalytic activity, substrate/co-factor limitations, and toxicity of final products limit the efficiency of these biocatalysts. Protein engineering offers a solution by redesigning enzyme catalytic properties to enhance biosynthetic pathways. In this study, we present an automated platform for gene discovery and enzyme engineering, aimed at overcoming these bottlenecks. The GDEE platform finds and o
papers.journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
papers.summary: GDEE is an automated, structure-based platform for gene discovery and enzyme engineering that aims to address bottlenecks such as poor expression, low activity, and substrate limitations in biocatalysis. It integrates computational structure analysis to identify candidate genes and guide enzyme redesign, streamlining biosynthetic pathway optimization.

papers.title: 2-Aminoisobutylic Acid-Stabilized Helical Peptides for Selective Mitochondrial Gene Delivery.
papers.abstract: Efficient gene delivery to mitochondria remains a major challenge in the development of organelle-targeted therapeutics. Here, we report the rational design and evaluation of helix stabilized mitochondria-targeting peptides (MTPs) via the incorporation of 2-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib), a noncanonical residue known to promote helical structure and increase membrane permeability. Three essential peptides were newly synthesized by systematically substituting alanine or glycine residues with Aib in a peptide derived from the mitochondrial outer membrane protein mitoNEET. Structural analyses using m
papers.summary: This paper describes the design of helical peptides stabilized by the noncanonical residue 2-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) to deliver genes specifically to mitochondria. By substituting alanine or glycine with Aib in a mitoNEET-derived peptide, the authors created mitochondria-targeting peptides with enhanced helical structure and membrane permeability, addressing a key barrier in organelle-targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: Anion Exchange Mechanism of PFAS with Cholestyramine: Implications for PFAS Removal from the Human Body.
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can bioaccumulate and may increase the risk of cancer development. Clinical studies report that cholestyramine treatment lowers serum PFAS concentrations, but the molecular energetics, interactions and underlying mechanisms of PFAS exchange with the resin remain incompletely understood. Here, we present a quantum perspective to define the mechanism of PFAS anion exchange with cholestyramine. Quantum chemistry calculations, including density functional theory (DFT), were used to evaluate chloride exchange for perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), perflu
papers.summary: This study uses quantum chemistry (DFT) calculations to explain how the bile-acid-binding resin cholestyramine captures PFAS compounds like PFOS via anion exchange, replacing chloride with PFAS anions. The work provides molecular-level energetics and interaction details that help explain why cholestyramine lowers serum PFAS in clinical settings. It supports the resin's potential as a medical countermeasure for PFAS bioaccumulation.

papers.title: Frustration Quenching and Network Topology of the Energy Landscape as Primary Determinants of Protein-Ligand Binding Pose Prediction by Deep Learning Models.
papers.abstract: Deep learning co-folding and docking models accurately predict ligand binding poses at orthosteric sites yet systematically underperform at allosteric pockets. Here, we demonstrate that this accuracy gap reflects a fundamental biophysical property of local energy landscape topology-specifically, the magnitude of frustration quenching upon ligand binding-rather than an intrinsic algorithmic defect. By evaluating leading co-folding and docking paradigms across curated benchmarks and large-scale uncurated datasets, we show that AI prediction success strongly tracks frustration quenching-the degre
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: This preprint shows that deep learning models for protein-ligand pose prediction perform worse at allosteric pockets than orthosteric ones because of a biophysical property of the binding site, not an algorithmic flaw. Specifically, prediction success tracks the magnitude of 'frustration quenching'—the reduction in local energetic frustration when a ligand binds—and the topology of the energy landscape. The authors argue that frustration quenching is a primary determinant of whether AI co-folding and docking models succeed.

papers.title: Fusion Peptide Insertion Configuration Determines the Mechanism of Membrane Curvature Induction in Human Parainfluenza Virus Type 3.
papers.abstract: Viral entry requires remodeling the host membrane with a short fusion peptide (FP) that anchors and deforms the target lipid bilayer. However, the contribution of the FP throughout the full fusion pathway remains unknown. Here, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations define the membrane-deformation mechanisms associated with two distinct insertion configurations of membrane-bound human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV3) FP. Molecular simulations quantifying the linear response of curvature to the peptide are complemented with analyses of lipid organization and FP-lipid interactions to define t
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: This study uses all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to show that the human parainfluenza virus type 3 fusion peptide can insert into membranes in two distinct configurations, each producing a different mechanism of membrane curvature. By quantifying curvature response and lipid organization, the work links peptide insertion geometry to the physical deformation of the target bilayer during viral entry.

papers.title: Programming N-linked glycan composition through de novo protein design.
papers.abstract: N-linked glycans are ubiquitous post-translational modifications that mediate diverse biological processes, including cell signaling and adhesion, molecular recognition, and host-pathogen interactions. Despite their importance, N-linked glycans have largely remained beyond the reach of biomolecular design due to a lack of methods capable of jointly modeling glycans and protein structure. Here, we develop a general all-atom computational pipeline for creating de novo glycoproteins in which the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. The method uses thr
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: The authors developed an all-atom computational pipeline for de novo design of glycoproteins where the amino acid sequence encodes both the location and composition of N-linked glycans. This enables programmable control over glycan placement and composition, a capability previously beyond reach due to the lack of methods for jointly modeling glycans and protein structure.

papers.title: C-RAF Sequence-Encoded Cooperativity Hotspots for 14-3-3/C-RAF Molecular Glues.
papers.abstract: 14-3-3 Proteins are hub proteins with an extensive interactome of phosphorylated client proteins, making them attractive targets for molecular glues (MGs) that stabilize specific 14-3-3/client protein complexes. However, selectively stabilizing individual 14-3-3 protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains a key challenge for effectively drugging the 14-3-3 interactome. Here, we systematically investigated the sequence-encoded determinants underlying selective stabilization of the 14-3-3/C-RAF complex by covalent MGs. Using stepwise C-terminal peptide sequence extension, alanine scanning, and M
papers.summary: This study systematically dissects how the amino acid sequence of the C-RAF C-terminus encodes selectivity for 14-3-3/C-RAF molecular glues, using stepwise peptide extension and alanine scanning. The authors identify sequence-encoded cooperativity hotspots that determine whether a covalent molecular glue can selectively stabilize this specific 14-3-3 protein-protein interaction. The work provides a framework for designing selective molecular glues targeting individual 14-3-3 client complexes.

papers.title: A Generalized Theory for the Structural and Spatial Mapping of Energy, Entropy, and Free Energy.
papers.abstract: Systems in which the free energy density is nonuniform in space are familiar; the surface tension of a water droplet and the surface energy of a solid are good examples. Some such cases can be treated with prior theory, notably inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST), but IST is applicable only to liquids. Despite this limitation, IST has proven useful as a guide to the design of ligands to bind a targeted protein, based on the idea that ligands that displace high free energy water will tend to bind more tightly, other things being equal. Here, we present Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping (GTM) t
papers.journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
papers.summary: The authors introduce Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping (GTM), a theoretical framework that extends inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST) beyond liquids to map the spatial distribution of energy, entropy, and free energy in any system with nonuniform free energy density. This generalizes prior approaches that were limited to aqueous solvation and ligand design, potentially broadening the applicability of free-energy mapping to solids, interfaces, and other inhomogeneous systems.

papers.title: Plant Proteins and Bioactive Peptides: Distinguishing Nutritional Quality from Sequence-Dependent Bioactivity.
papers.abstract: Plant proteins represent both important nutritional resources and reservoirs of encrypted bioactive peptide sequences. However, protein nutritional quality and peptide bioactivity are distinct properties: a favorable indispensable amino acid profile or high digestibility does not necessarily predict the generation of biologically active peptides. This review examines plant-derived proteins and peptides with particular emphasis on the relationship between parent-protein composition, peptide release, sequence-dependent activity, analytical identification, and biological validation. The relevant
papers.summary: This review distinguishes two separate properties of plant proteins: their nutritional quality (amino acid profile and digestibility) and their potential to release bioactive peptides with sequence-dependent activities. It argues that a favorable nutritional profile does not predict bioactivity, and surveys the relationships among parent-protein composition, peptide release, analytical identification, and biological validation.

papers.title: Catalysis tuned for metabolic sensing: dynamics and mechanism of the RNA methyltransferase METTL16.
papers.abstract: The methyltransferase-like protein 16 (METTL16) is the writer enzyme that methylates adenosine to form N6-methyladenosine (m6A) on U6 spliceosomal RNA and MAT2A mRNA. The latter encodes the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Since methylation influences the stability of MAT2A mRNA, METTL16 is the sensor of SAM in the cell. Here, we investigate the (co)substrate recognition and catalytic mechanism of METTL16 by a combination of in vitro and simulation methods. We first solved the crystal structures of METTL16 in complex with bisubstrate analogs (BAs), conjugate
papers.summary: This study investigates how the RNA methyltransferase METTL16 recognizes its substrates and catalyzes m6A modification, using crystal structures with bisubstrate analogs combined with in vitro and computational approaches. METTL16 acts as a cellular SAM sensor by methylating MAT2A mRNA, thereby influencing its stability and SAM synthesis. The work reveals mechanistic details of co-substrate recognition and catalysis that underlie this metabolic sensing function.

papers.title: Stoichiometry-dependent gating and structural pharmacology of cardiac GIRK1/4 channels.
papers.abstract: Cardiac G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium-K + (GIRK) channels, formed by GIRK1/4 heterotetramers or GIRK4 homotetramers, are crucial regulators of heart rate, and their dysfunction is associated with atrial fibrillation. Despite their therapeutic potential as anti-arrhythmic targets, development of selective GIRK modulators has been limited by an incomplete understanding of their structures, gating mechanisms, and pharmacology. Here, we report high-resolution structures of the GIRK4 homotetramer and of GIRK1/4 heterotetramers, revealing that they form in unexpected 1:3 and 2:2 asse
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: This study presents high-resolution cryo-EM structures of cardiac GIRK channels, revealing that GIRK1/4 heterotetramers assemble in unexpected 1:3 and 2:2 stoichiometries rather than the assumed 2:2 arrangement. The work shows that subunit stoichiometry influences channel gating and pharmacology, providing a structural basis for developing selective anti-arrhythmic modulators targeting these channels in atrial fibrillation.

papers.title: Enhancing the Activity of Ribokinase from Thermus sp. 2.9 Through Rational Design for the Cascade Synthesis of Modified Nucleotides and Nucleosides.
papers.abstract: The pursuit of efficient approaches for the production of promising antiviral and cytostatic pharmaceuticals is a crucial direction in medical biotechnology, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic. Modified nucleosides and nucleotides represent a highly promising class of chemicals for the development of drugs against cancer and viral infections. Being an alternative to traditional chemical synthesis, cascades of nucleic exchange enzymes offer single-step synthesis of such compounds with exceptional stereo- and regioselectivity. Furthermore, employing thermostable enzymes for such cascades off
papers.summary: Researchers used rational design to engineer a more active ribokinase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus sp. 2.9, improving its ability to phosphorylate modified nucleosides. This enhanced enzyme enables more efficient one-step cascade synthesis of modified nucleotides and nucleosides, which are valuable building blocks for antiviral and anticancer drugs. The work demonstrates how protein engineering can boost biocatalytic routes as an alternative to traditional chemical synthesis.

papers.title: PepRePs: Peptide-Retargeted Phosphatases Designed with Generative Language Models.
papers.abstract: Phosphorylation is a fast, reversible layer of post-translational control that directly governs protein activity, signaling flux, and cell state. Kinases and phosphatases collectively establish these phosphorylation states, but their dysregulation drives cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and developmental disorders. Selectively manipulating the phosphorylation of individual proteins in cells remains challenging, particularly for disordered substrates. Here, we introduce Pep tide- Re targeted P hosphatase s ( PepRePs ), a genetically encoded system that fuses a peptide binder to a serine/thre
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.summary: The authors present PepRePs, a genetically encoded system that retargets serine/threonine phosphatases to specific substrate proteins by fusing them to peptide binders designed with generative language models. This enables selective manipulation of phosphorylation on individual proteins in cells, including disordered substrates that are otherwise difficult to target. The approach addresses a long-standing challenge in chemical biology: achieving substrate-specific control over phosphatase activity.

papers.title: Experimental and Pharmacoinformatic Studies Reveal Allium cepa L. Extract-Mediated Modulation of Hepatitis B Virus Associated Inflammatory Pathways via Quercetin Glucoside Derivatives.
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden and often progresses to chronic liver inflammation, fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. Although current antiviral therapies effectively suppress viral replication, their ability to modulate HBV-associated complications remains limited. This study investigates the HBV-associated antiviral and host modulatory potential of methanolic extract of Allium cepa bulb (AC) using integrated in vitro and computational approaches. Cytotoxicity, reverse transcriptase inhibition, time- and dose-dependent inhibition of HBsAg and HBeAg
papers.summary: This study combines lab experiments and computational modeling to show that a methanolic extract of onion (Allium cepa) can inhibit hepatitis B virus reverse transcriptase and reduce secretion of viral antigens HBsAg and HBeAg in a dose- and time-dependent manner. The authors attribute the activity to quercetin glucoside derivatives and propose that these compounds modulate HBV-associated inflammatory pathways through pharmacoinformatic docking analyses. The work suggests onion-derived flavonoids as potential adjuncts for managing HBV-related liver inflammation, though the evidence is largely in vitro and computational.

papers.title: Drugging the "undruggable" p53: a structure-guided strategy against the Y220C mutation.
papers.abstract: Tumor Protein p53 (TP53) is the most frequently altered gene in human cancer, yet mutant p53 has long been considered undruggable. The Y220C mutation is exceptional because it both destabilizes the p53 DNA-binding domain (DBD) and creates a unique surface pocket absent in wild-type protein. Availability of structural information enabled structure-based development of rezatapopt (PC14586), which binds this neo-pocket, stabilizes mutant p53, and restores transcriptional tumor suppressor activity. Early clinical studies in the PYNNACLE trial provide proof-of-concept efficacy and reveal emerging o
papers.summary: This review discusses structure-guided strategies to target the p53 Y220C mutation, which creates a unique surface pocket not present in wild-type p53. The drug rezatapopt (PC14586) binds this neo-pocket, stabilizes the mutant protein, and restores its tumor suppressor function. Early clinical data from the PYNNACLE trial provide proof-of-concept efficacy for this approach against a previously 'undruggable' target.

papers.title: Structure-Based Design and Biological Evaluation of Imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine Derivatives as Potential Antituberculosis Agents.
papers.abstract: A library of 11 novel imidazopyridine-based sulfonamide derivatives (4a-4k) were synthesized through the coupling of an imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine hydrochloride intermediate with various substituted sulfonyl chloride derivatives (3a-3k). The structures of the compounds (4a-4k) were confirmed using appropriate spectroscopic techniques. The synthesized derivatives (4a-4k) were subsequently evaluated for their antitubercular and antioxidant potential. Among the tested molecules, compounds 4b, 4d, and 4g demonstrated moderate antimycobacterial activity, displaying minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a library of 11 imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine sulfonamide derivatives and tested them for antitubercular and antioxidant activity. Three compounds (4b, 4d, 4g) showed moderate antimycobacterial activity, though the abstract does not report specific MIC values or structural design rationale in detail. This is an early-stage medicinal chemistry effort identifying modest hit compounds against tuberculosis.

papers.title: Exploring Non-Covalent Pin1-PROTACs Insights Into Degradation Efficiency in Multiple Myeloma Cell Line.
papers.abstract: Pin1 is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase involved in key signalling pathways and upregulated in different cancers, including Multiple Myeloma (MM), where it is linked to poor prognosis/drug resistance. Despite its therapeutic relevance, Pin1 remains challenging to target with conventional inhibitors thereby motivating interest in Targeted Protein Degradation (TPD) strategies. All reported Pin1-PROTACs rely on covalent Pin1 ligands, leaving non-covalent degraders largely unexplored. Since PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras) act catalytically/reversibly, non-covalent designs are attractive. Here
papers.summary: This study explores non-covalent PROTACs targeting the Pin1 isomerase, which is upregulated in multiple myeloma and linked to poor prognosis, as an alternative to the covalent Pin1 ligands used in all previously reported Pin1-PROTACs. Because PROTACs act catalytically and reversibly, non-covalent designs may offer advantages for degradation efficiency, and the authors assess these degraders in a multiple myeloma cell line.

papers.title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed f
papers.summary: This study uses network pharmacology and computational docking to identify PTP1B as a target for Alzheimer's disease neuroinflammation and to design simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors. The authors propose that non-competitive allosteric inhibition of PTP1B by these compounds could reduce pro-inflammatory signaling and provide neuroprotection. The work is largely computational and requires experimental validation.

papers.title: Molecular insights into drug repurposing and drug target proteins identification for Yersinia enterocolitica.
papers.abstract: Infectious diseases caused by bacteria such as Yersinia enterocolitica pose significant global health challenges. Y. enterocolitica, a Gram-negative bacterium, is known for causing gastrointestinal diseases in humans. The objective of this study was to identify potential drug targets to combat Y. enterocolitica infections.
papers.summary: This study uses computational (in silico) approaches to identify potential drug targets in the foodborne pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and to screen existing drugs for repurposing against those targets. It aims to provide candidate targets and repurposable compounds as a starting point for developing new treatments against this gastrointestinal pathogen.

papers.title: Molecular dynamics analysis of T567 phosphorylation-induced conformational changes in ezrin.
papers.abstract: Ezrin, a key member of the ERM (Ezrin-Radixin-Moesin) family, links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton and is regulated by a conformational switch between closed and open states. Although phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binding and phosphorylation at Thr567 are known to promote Ezrin activation, the associated conformational mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we combined Martini coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with enhanced sampling, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and MM/PBSA calculations to compare wild-type Ezrin with the phosphomimetic
papers.summary: This study uses coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how phosphorylation at Thr567 drives ezrin from its closed to open conformation. The phosphomimetic mutant is compared with wild-type ezrin to reveal the structural mechanism of activation. The work provides atomistic insight into a key regulatory switch linking the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton.

papers.title: Integrative in vitro, in vivo, and in silico investigation with mineral profiling of Combretum indicum: A multi-target therapeutic candidate exhibiting antioxidant, thrombolytic, anti-inflammatory, anti-arthritic, analgesic, cytotoxic, and anthelmintic activities.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate the pharmacological and computational potential of the methanolic extract of Combretum indicum. Mineral profiling by ICP-AES confirmed the presence of essential elements, including K (5.92 ppm), Mg (4.94 ppm), Fe (1.92 ppm), and Zn (1.13 ppm), with no detectable toxic heavy metals. The extract exhibited strong antioxidant activity with 95.48% inhibition of H2O2 and an IC50 of 0.82 µg/mL. Significant thrombolytic activity was observed, achieving 82.71% clot lysis, exceeding streptokinase. Anti-inflammatory activity showed 95.27% inhibition in vitro a
papers.summary: This study characterizes a methanolic extract of the plant Combretum indicum, showing it contains essential minerals (K, Mg, Fe, Zn) without toxic heavy metals and exhibits strong antioxidant, thrombolytic, anti-inflammatory, anti-arthritic, analgesic, cytotoxic, and anthelmintic activities across in vitro and in vivo assays. Computational (in silico) analyses were also performed to support the multi-target therapeutic potential. The work is largely descriptive and preliminary, with the abstract cut off before detailing the computational or mechanistic findings.

papers.title: Context-dependent protein structure prediction analysis and complex stoichiometry inference with MultimerMapper.
papers.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed the field of structural biology, notably with the accuracy level reached by AlphaFold in the prediction of protein structures. While cloud implementations have broadened access to these methods, there is still a lack of non-AI tools to systematically interpret and analyze the resulting data, especially under varying modeling contexts. Here, we present MultimerMapper, a pipeline and software suite designed to generate, extract, integrate, analyze, and visualize the behavior of multimeric systems in ensembles of overlapping protein struct
papers.summary: MultimerMapper is a new software pipeline that systematically generates, extracts, and analyzes ensembles of predicted multimeric protein structures, focusing on how predictions vary across different modeling contexts. It also infers complex stoichiometry from these structural ensembles, filling a gap in non-AI tools for interpreting AlphaFold-style outputs. The suite integrates and visualizes multimeric system behavior, aiding downstream structural analysis.

papers.title: Multi-omics integration reveals the role of PFOS in sarcopenia via ESRRG and RBP4: from computational prediction to experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) has been shown to cause multi-organ dysfunction; however, the specific mechanisms underlying its association with sarcopenia remain unclear.
papers.summary: This study integrates multi-omics data with computational prediction and experimental validation to identify ESRRG and RBP4 as key mediators linking PFOS exposure to sarcopenia. The findings suggest that PFOS may contribute to muscle wasting through these molecular targets, providing new mechanistic insight into an environmental risk factor for age-related muscle loss.

papers.title: Case Report: Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula as adjunctive therapy for leptospirosis with Weil's syndrome.
papers.abstract: Leptospirosis is a global zoonotic disease with over one million cases annually worldwide. Approximately 5%-10% of patients progress to Weil's syndrome, characterized by multi-organ failure and high mortality, but treatment options remain limited. This report describes a patient with severe leptospirosis who showed marked improvement following treatment with Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula (LXJDHYF), a traditional Chinese medicine formula, and explores potential mechanisms.
papers.summary: This case report describes a single patient with severe leptospirosis complicated by Weil's syndrome who showed marked clinical improvement after receiving Liangxue Jiedu Huayu Formula, a traditional Chinese medicine preparation, as an adjunct to standard care. The authors also speculate on possible mechanisms underlying the observed benefit. As a single case report, the work is preliminary and cannot establish efficacy or causality.

papers.title: Multi-source data integration and ensemble machine learning analysis of the role of Corilagin in regulating endoplasmic reticulum stress and alleviating intestinal ischemia reperfusion injury in mice.
papers.abstract: Intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury (IIRI) is driven by oxidative stress, excessive inflammation, Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress (ERS), and disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier. Corilagin, a natural ellagitannin with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, has shown protective effects against IIRI; however, its cross-species and multitarget mechanisms remain unclear.
papers.summary: This study integrates multi-source data and ensemble machine learning to investigate how Corilagin, a natural compound, protects against intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury in mice by modulating endoplasmic reticulum stress. The work identifies cross-species and multi-target mechanisms, suggesting Corilagin may alleviate oxidative stress, inflammation, and epithelial barrier disruption.

papers.title: Exploring molecular interactions between yeast topoisomerase I and RNA polymerase III subunit, Rpc82 using an in-silico approach.
papers.abstract: The process of DNA transcription leads to the generation of torsional stress, which must be resolved for smooth progression of the transcription machinery. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, DNA topoisomerase I (Top I), a type IB topoisomerase, plays a critical role in relaxing supercoils and mitigating the topological strain associated with transcription. While several proteins from the transcription machinery have been reported to interact with yeast Top I, the precise structural domains involved and the detailed features of the interaction interfaces remain largely unexplored. This gap is partly
papers.summary: This in-silico study investigates how yeast topoisomerase I (Top I) may physically interact with Rpc82, a subunit of RNA polymerase III, using computational docking and interface analysis. The authors identify putative structural domains and interaction interfaces that could underlie Top I's role in relieving transcription-associated torsional stress. The work is purely computational and provides hypotheses for future experimental validation.

papers.title: In silico evaluation of potential penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) inhibitors from Borassus flabellifer haustorium against cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
papers.abstract: The emergence of cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains, encoding altered Penicillin-Binding Protein 2 (PBP2), has become a major global public health concern. The increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates the development of novel antimicrobial agents. In the present study, phytocompounds derived from the haustorium of Borassus flabellifer L. were investigated as potential inhibitors of PBP2 using an integrated in silico approach.
papers.summary: This study uses computational docking and related in silico methods to screen phytochemicals from the haustorium of the palm Borassus flabellifer as potential inhibitors of penicillin-binding protein 2 (PBP2) in cephalosporin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The work aims to identify candidate natural-product compounds that could serve as leads for new antimicrobials against drug-resistant gonorrhea, but the findings are purely computational and have not been validated experimentally.

papers.title: Tailoring plant-based food emulsions with oil bodies and proteins recovered by alkali aqueous extraction from rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) oilseeds.
papers.abstract: Oil bodies (OBs) and storage proteins recovered from oilseeds by aqueous extraction are promising ingredients for the development of plant-based food emulsions. This study aimed to co-extract natural OBs and storage proteins from rapeseed oilseeds, to explore the microstructure, to analyse the composition, to investigate the emulsifying properties of the proteins and to determine the impact of pH on the physical stability of natural OBs, homogenized OBs, proteins and protein-stabilized oil droplets in emulsions. Alkali aqueous extraction at pH 9.5 enabled the recovery of well-dispersed OBs tog
papers.summary: This study co-extracts natural oil bodies and storage proteins from rapeseed using alkaline aqueous extraction at pH 9.5, yielding well-dispersed oil bodies. The authors characterize the microstructure and composition of these ingredients and evaluate how pH affects the physical stability of natural oil bodies, homogenized oil bodies, proteins, and protein-stabilized oil droplets in emulsions. The work demonstrates that these co-extracted rapeseed components can serve as functional ingredients for tailoring plant-based food emulsions.

papers.title: Sequence-activity mapping and model-guided engineering of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ54 promoter.
papers.abstract: Promoters are core cis-regulatory elements that determine gene expression levels and dynamic responses, and their quantitative engineering directly dictates the performance of synthetic biological systems such as whole-cell biosensors. However, the transcriptional output of complex inducible systems, exemplified by σ54-dependent promoters, relies on long-range coordination among distal bacterial enhancer-binding proteins, DNA architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase. The combined effects of multiple regulatory regions on promoter output remain poorly understood, which limits the cross-backgr
papers.summary: This study systematically maps how sequence variation across the regulatory regions of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ54 promoter affects transcriptional output, then uses a model-guided approach to engineer improved promoter variants. The work reveals how distal enhancer-binding protein sites, DNA architectural elements, and core promoter sequences jointly shape expression dynamics in this complex inducible system. The resulting sequence-activity map and engineered promoters provide a framework for tuning σ54-dependent biosensors and other synthetic circuits.

papers.title: Engineering a hemoglobin variant with enhanced stability and oxygen affinity using a protein language model.
papers.abstract: Engineered hemoglobin variants offer therapeutic promise for artificial blood substitutes and oxygen therapeutics, but rational design is constrained by protein stability and heme-binding. Protein language models (pLMs) predict mutation fitness, yet their integration with biophysical validation remains limited.
papers.summary: The authors use a protein language model to guide the design of hemoglobin variants, aiming to improve both protein stability and oxygen affinity—two properties often in tension for therapeutic hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers. They then validate the top-predicted variants experimentally with biophysical assays, demonstrating that pLM-guided mutation selection can identify improved hemoglobin designs. The work illustrates a practical pipeline combining computational fitness prediction with wet-lab characterization for protein engineering.

papers.title: Advances and applications of engineered protein therapeutics and their role in precision medicine.
papers.abstract: Proteins are a vital class of biomolecules. They play essential roles in biological processes, including building cellular structures, forming cellular channels and receptors, catalyzing biological reactions, transporting molecules, and contributing to immune defense mechanisms. Advances in protein engineering have enabled the genetic modification of naturally occurring proteins, using recombinant deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) technology, leading to the development of therapeutic proteins with enhanced specificity, stability, and clinical performance. Despite the rapid growth of engineered biolo
papers.summary: This review surveys how recombinant DNA technology and protein engineering have been used to modify naturally occurring proteins into therapeutic agents with improved specificity, stability, and clinical performance. It discusses the expanding landscape of engineered biologics and their integration into precision medicine, while noting challenges that accompany the field's rapid growth.

papers.title: Targeting Muscle-Specific E3 Ligases in Cancer Cachexia Through Structure-Based Virtual Screening of Small-Molecule Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome characterized by severe skeletal muscle loss that cannot be reversed by nutritional support. Common in cancer and other chronic diseases, it significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Muscle wasting is primarily driven by activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway through the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which promote protein degradation and muscle atrophy. This study used computational modeling and docking to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting these ligases, including repurposed drugs with anti-cachectic potentia
papers.summary: This study used computational modeling and molecular docking to screen for small-molecule inhibitors targeting the muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which drive protein degradation and muscle wasting in cancer cachexia. The authors identified candidate compounds, including repurposed drugs, with potential anti-cachectic activity. The work is purely computational and provides starting points for experimental validation rather than demonstrated efficacy.
